title: Articles & Noun Gender
summary: Every German noun carries a gender, and the article is the only reliable signal of it.
bodyMd:
German has three genders, and they are a property of the **word**, not the thing. `das Mädchen` (girl) is neuter because of its `-chen` ending, not because of anything about girls.

That is why you should never learn a noun on its own. Learn **der Hund**, not *Hund*. The article is part of the word.

## The nominative articles

| masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|
| **der** Hund | **die** Katze | **das** Haus | **die** Häuser |

The plural article is always `die`, whatever the singular gender was.

## Endings that give the gender away

About a third of nouns announce their gender through their ending:

- **die** — `-ung`, `-heit`, `-keit`, `-schaft`, `-ion`, `-tät`, `-ei`
- **das** — `-chen`, `-lein`, `-ment`, `-um`, `-ma`
- **der** — `-er` (person doing something), `-ling`, `-ismus`

Days, months, seasons and weather words are **der**: der Montag, der Mai, der Sommer, der Regen.
keyRules: Learn every noun together with its article — der Hund, not Hund.
All plurals take die in the nominative, regardless of singular gender.
-ung / -heit / -keit / -schaft / -ion are always feminine.
-chen and -lein are always neuter, even for people: das Mädchen.

examples.en: The girl is reading a book.

title: The Present Tense
summary: One tense does the work of three in English — and it covers the future too.
bodyMd:
German `ich lerne` covers English *I learn*, *I am learning* and *I do learn*. There is no separate continuous form to worry about.

## Regular endings

Drop `-en` from the infinitive and add:

| | lernen |
|---|---|
| ich | lern**e** |
| du | lern**st** |
| er/sie/es | lern**t** |
| wir | lern**en** |
| ihr | lern**t** |
| sie/Sie | lern**en** |

If the stem ends in `-t` or `-d`, slip in an **e** so it stays pronounceable: `du arbeit**e**st`, `er arbeit**e**t`.

## Stem-changing verbs

A group of common verbs change their stem vowel — but **only** in the `du` and `er/sie/es` forms:

| change | infinitive | du | er/sie/es |
|---|---|---|---|
| e → i | sprechen | sprichst | spricht |
| e → ie | sehen | siehst | sieht |
| a → ä | fahren | fährst | fährt |
| au → äu | laufen | läufst | läuft |

Everything else stays regular: `wir sprechen`, `ihr sprecht`.

## The present tense as future

With a time expression, the present tense is the normal way to talk about the future:

`**Morgen fahre** ich nach Berlin.` — *Tomorrow I'm going to Berlin.*
keyRules: Drop -en, add -e / -st / -t / -en / -t / -en.
Stems ending in -t or -d insert an e: du arbeitest.
Stem changes affect only the du and er/sie/es forms.
wir and sie/Sie forms are always identical to the infinitive.
German uses the present tense for the future when a time word makes it clear.

examples.en: He is going to Hamburg tomorrow.

title: Nominative & Accusative
summary: Who is doing it, and who is having it done to them.
bodyMd:
German marks a noun's job in the sentence by changing the article in front of it. The first two jobs to learn:

- **Nominative** — the subject, the one doing the verb.
- **Accusative** — the direct object, the one on the receiving end.

`**Der Hund** (nom) beißt **den Mann** (akk).` — the dog bites the man.
`**Den Hund** (akk) beißt **der Mann** (nom).` — the *man* bites the dog.

Notice that the word order flipped but the meaning is carried by the articles, not the positions. This is what cases buy you.

## The good news

| | masc | fem | neut | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nominative | der | die | das | die |
| Accusative | **den** | die | das | die |

**Only the masculine changes.** Feminine, neuter and plural look identical in both cases.

The same `-n` appears on `ein → einen` and `kein → keinen`, and on the possessives: `mein → meinen`.

## After sein, it stays nominative

`sein`, `werden` and `bleiben` don't take an object — they link two halves of an equation, so both sides are nominative:

`Er ist **ein guter Lehrer**.` (not *einen*)
keyRules: Nominative = subject; accusative = direct object.
Only masculine articles change: der becomes den.
ein → einen, kein → keinen, mein → meinen in the masculine accusative.
sein, werden and bleiben are followed by the nominative, not the accusative.

title: Word Order: Verb Second
summary: The single most important rule in German sentence structure.
bodyMd:
In a German statement the conjugated verb sits in **position two**. Not the second word — the second *element*.

`**Ich** | **gehe** | heute ins Kino.`
`**Heute** | **gehe** | ich ins Kino.`

Front anything you like for emphasis, and the subject simply hops behind the verb. The verb itself never moves.

## Questions

- **Yes/no** — verb first: `**Gehst** du ins Kino?`
- **W-question** — question word first, verb second: `Wann **gehst** du ins Kino?`

## What goes at the end

German brackets its sentences. The conjugated verb is in position 2, and anything else verbal is parked at the very end:

- separable prefix — `Ich **stehe** um sieben Uhr **auf**.`
- infinitive after a modal — `Ich **kann** heute nicht **kommen**.`
- past participle — `Ich **habe** gestern Fußball **gespielt**.`

## Order of the middle

When several details pile up, the default is **Time – Manner – Place**:

`Ich fahre **morgen** **mit dem Bus** **nach Berlin**.`
keyRules: The conjugated verb is always the second element in a statement.
Fronting another element pushes the subject after the verb — the verb stays put.
Yes/no questions start with the verb; W-questions put the verb second.
Separable prefixes, infinitives and participles go to the very end.
Middle-field order is Time – Manner – Place.

examples.en: Today I'm going to the cinema.

examples.de: Wir fahren morgen mit dem Zug nach Köln.
examples.en: We're travelling to Cologne by train tomorrow.

title: Negation: nicht and kein
summary: Two ways to say no, and a clear rule for choosing between them.
bodyMd:
## kein negates nouns

Use **kein** wherever you would have said `ein` — or where there was no article at all:

`Ich habe **ein** Auto.` → `Ich habe **kein** Auto.`
`Ich trinke Kaffee.` → `Ich trinke **keinen** Kaffee.`

`kein` declines exactly like `ein`: kein / keine / kein, accusative masculine **keinen**.

## nicht negates everything else

If the noun has a **definite** article or a possessive, or if you're negating a verb, adjective or phrase, use **nicht**:

`Ich kenne **den** Mann **nicht**.`
`Das ist **nicht** gut.`

## Where nicht goes

`nicht` comes **before** the thing it negates:

- before an adjective — `Das ist **nicht** teuer.`
- before a prepositional phrase — `Ich fahre **nicht** nach Berlin.`
- before a separable prefix — `Ich stehe **nicht** auf.`

But it comes **after** a definite direct object, and after time expressions:

`Ich kenne den Mann **nicht**.`
`Ich komme heute **nicht**.`
keyRules: kein replaces ein, or a bare noun with no article.
nicht negates verbs, adjectives, and nouns that have a definite article.
kein declines like ein: keinen in the masculine accusative.
nicht goes before adjectives and prepositional phrases, but after a definite object.

title: The Perfect Tense
summary: How Germans actually talk about the past.
bodyMd:
In conversation the Perfekt does nearly all the past-tense work, even for things English would put in the simple past.

**Structure**: a helper verb in position 2, the participle at the very end.

`Ich **habe** gestern Fußball **gespielt**.`

## Building the participle

| Type | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| regular | **ge** + stem + **t** | spielen → gespielt |
| irregular | **ge** + stem + **en** | sehen → gesehen |
| separable | prefix + **ge** + rest | aufstehen → aufgestanden |
| ends in -ieren | **no ge-** | studieren → studiert |
| inseparable prefix | **no ge-** | verstehen → verstanden |

The inseparable prefixes are **be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss-, ver-, zer-**. None of them take `ge-`.

## haben or sein?

Most verbs take **haben**. Use **sein** when the verb involves:

1. **movement from A to B** — gehen, fahren, fliegen, kommen, laufen
2. **a change of state** — aufstehen, einschlafen, sterben, werden
3. the three memorised exceptions — **sein, bleiben, passieren**

`Ich **bin** nach Berlin **gefahren**.` but `Ich **habe** das Auto **gefahren**.` — with a direct object, `fahren` switches to haben.
keyRules: Perfekt = haben/sein (position 2) + Partizip II (final position).
Regular participles are ge- + stem + -t; irregular ones end in -en.
Verbs in -ieren and verbs with inseparable prefixes take no ge-.
Use sein for motion, change of state, and sein/bleiben/passieren.
Separable verbs slot ge- between prefix and stem: aufgestanden.

examples.de: Sie ist um sieben Uhr aufgestanden.

title: The Dative Case
summary: The third case: the receiver, and the one prepositions love.
bodyMd:
The dative marks the **indirect object** — the person something is given, said or shown to.

`Ich gebe **dem Kind** einen Apfel.` — *to the child*.

## The articles

| | masc | fem | neut | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dative | **dem** | **der** | **dem** | **den** + noun**-n** |

Two things to watch:
- Feminine `die` becomes **der** — the same word as the masculine nominative. Context tells them apart.
- The **plural noun itself** takes an `-n`: `mit den Kinder**n**`, `mit den Freund**en**`.

## Verbs that demand the dative

Some verbs take a dative object where English uses a plain direct object. These simply have to be memorised:

**helfen, danken, gefallen, gehören, antworten, folgen, glauben, passen, schmecken, gratulieren**

`Ich helfe **dir**.` — *I help you*, not *I help to you*.
`Das Buch gehört **mir**.`
`Das Essen schmeckt **mir** gut.`

## Two objects

When a sentence has both, the order is **dative before accusative** — unless the accusative is a pronoun, which jumps in front:

`Ich gebe **dem Mann** **das Buch**.`
`Ich gebe **es** **dem Mann**.`
keyRules: Dative marks the indirect object — the receiver.
Feminine die becomes der in the dative.
Dative plural adds -n to the noun itself: mit den Kindern.
helfen, danken, gefallen, gehören and friends take a dative object.
Dative comes before accusative, unless the accusative is a pronoun.

examples.en: The book belongs to the teacher.

examples.de: Er gibt den Kindern die Bücher.
examples.en: He gives the children the books.

title: Modal Verbs
summary: Six verbs that reshape the whole sentence around them.
bodyMd:
Modals express possibility, obligation, permission and desire. They are conjugated in position 2, and they send the main verb to the **end as a bare infinitive**.

`Ich **kann** heute nicht **kommen**.`

## The forms

| | können | müssen | dürfen | wollen | sollen | mögen |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | kann | muss | darf | will | soll | mag |
| du | kannst | musst | darfst | willst | sollst | magst |
| er/sie/es | kann | muss | darf | will | soll | mag |
| wir | können | müssen | dürfen | wollen | sollen | mögen |
| ihr | könnt | müsst | dürft | wollt | sollt | mögt |
| sie/Sie | können | müssen | dürfen | wollen | sollen | mögen |

Two quirks worth burning in: **ich** and **er/sie/es** are identical, and neither takes an ending.

## The trap: negated müssen

This one catches every learner:

- `Du **musst nicht** kommen.` = You **don't have to** come.
- `Du **darfst nicht** kommen.` = You **must not** come.

For English *must not*, you need **nicht dürfen**.

## möchte

`möchte` (*would like*) is technically the subjunctive of mögen, but it behaves as its own verb and is far more polite than `wollen`:

`Ich **möchte** einen Kaffee, bitte.`
keyRules: The modal takes position 2; the main verb goes to the end as an infinitive.
ich and er/sie/es forms are identical and take no ending.
nicht müssen = don't have to; nicht dürfen = must not.
Use möchte rather than wollen to sound polite.
Modals drop their umlaut in the Präteritum: können → konnte.

title: Prepositions and Their Cases
summary: Every preposition locks its noun into a case. Some pick one depending on meaning.
bodyMd:
## Fixed-case prepositions

**Always accusative**: `durch, für, gegen, ohne, um, bis, entlang`
**Always dative**: `aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu, gegenüber`

These never vary. Learn them as blocks.

## The two-way prepositions

Nine prepositions take **either** case, and the choice carries meaning:

`an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen`

| Question | Case | Sense |
|---|---|---|
| **Wohin?** (where to) | accusative | movement into a new place |
| **Wo?** (where) | dative | staying put |

`Ich gehe **in die** Schule.` — movement, accusative.
`Ich bin **in der** Schule.` — location, dative.

The test is not whether the verb involves motion — it's whether the motion **crosses into** the place:

`Ich laufe **in dem** Park.` (running around inside it — dative)
`Ich laufe **in den** Park.` (running into it — accusative)

## Contractions

Certain combinations are always contracted in normal German:

`in dem → **im**` · `in das → **ins**` · `an dem → **am**` · `an das → **ans**` · `zu dem → **zum**` · `zu der → **zur**` · `bei dem → **beim**` · `von dem → **vom**`
keyRules: durch, für, gegen, ohne, um always take the accusative.
aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu always take the dative.
Two-way prepositions take accusative for Wohin? and dative for Wo?.
The test is whether movement crosses into the place, not whether motion occurs.
Contract in dem → im, zu der → zur, an das → ans and friends.

examples.de: Wir fahren mit dem Auto zum Bahnhof.
examples.en: We're driving to the station by car.

title: Comparative & Superlative
summary: Making comparisons, including the ones that trip English speakers up.
bodyMd:
German always builds comparatives with an ending — there is no *more beautiful* construction.

| Positive | Comparative | Superlative |
|---|---|---|
| schnell | schnell**er** | am schnell**sten** |
| schön | schön**er** | am schön**sten** |

Even long adjectives follow this: `interessant → interessanter`, never *mehr interessant*.

## Umlauts

Most one-syllable adjectives with **a, o, u** add an umlaut:

`alt → **ä**lter` · `groß → gr**ö**ßer` · `jung → j**ü**nger` · `lang → l**ä**nger`

## The -est- insert

Stems ending in `-d`, `-t`, `-s`, `-ß`, `-z` insert an **e** in the superlative so it can be pronounced:

`alt → am ält**e**sten` · `heiß → am heiß**e**sten`

## Irregulars

| | comparative | superlative |
|---|---|---|
| gut | besser | am besten |
| viel | mehr | am meisten |
| gern | lieber | am liebsten |
| hoch | höher | am höchsten |
| nah | näher | am nächsten |

## wie or als?

- **so … wie** for things that are equal: `Er ist **so groß wie** ich.`
- **als** for a difference: `Er ist größer **als** ich.`

Using `wie` for a difference is the single most common mistake here.
keyRules: Comparatives always add -er; German has no 'mehr + adjective' form.
One-syllable adjectives with a, o, u usually take an umlaut.
Stems in -d, -t, -s, -ß, -z insert an e: am ältesten.
gut → besser → am besten; viel → mehr → am meisten; gern → lieber → am liebsten.
so … wie for equality, als for difference.

examples.de: Mein Bruder ist älter als ich.
examples.en: My brother is older than me.

examples.de: Sie ist so groß wie ihre Mutter.
examples.en: She is as tall as her mother.

examples.de: Das ist der beste Film des Jahres.
examples.en: That's the best film of the year.

title: Subordinate Clauses
summary: When the verb goes to the end — and which connectors send it there.
bodyMd:
A subordinating conjunction pushes the conjugated verb to the **very end** of its clause:

`Ich bleibe zu Hause, **weil** ich krank **bin**.`

The common subordinators: **weil, dass, wenn, ob, obwohl, damit, bevor, nachdem, während, seitdem, als, falls**.

## The weil / denn trap

Both mean *because*, but they behave completely differently:

`Ich bleibe zu Hause, **weil** ich krank **bin**.` — verb last
`Ich bleibe zu Hause, **denn** ich **bin** krank.` — normal order

`denn` is a **coordinating** conjunction, like `und`, `aber`, `oder` and `sondern`. None of those five change the word order.

## wenn or als?

- **als** — one completed event in the past: `**Als** ich zehn war, zogen wir um.`
- **wenn** — repeated past events, or anything present or future: `**Wenn** es regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause.`

If you can say *whenever*, use `wenn`. If it happened exactly once in the past, use `als`.

## Leading with the subordinate clause

Put the subordinate clause first and the whole thing counts as position one — so the main clause must start with its verb:

`**Weil** ich krank **bin**, **bleibe** ich zu Hause.`

The two verbs end up next to each other, separated by a comma. That looks strange at first but is correct.
keyRules: Subordinating conjunctions send the conjugated verb to the end of the clause.
weil sends the verb last; denn does not change word order.
und, aber, oder, denn, sondern never affect word order.
als = a single past event; wenn = repeated past, or present/future.
A fronted subordinate clause forces the main clause to begin with its verb.

examples.de: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Berlin wohne.
examples.en: I'm learning German because I live in Berlin.

examples.de: Als ich Kind war, spielte ich Fußball.
examples.en: When I was a child, I played football.

examples.de: Wenn ich Zeit habe, besuche ich dich.
examples.en: When I have time, I'll visit you.

title: Adjective Endings
summary: The table everyone dreads — and the shortcut that makes it manageable.
bodyMd:
An adjective in front of a noun must take an ending. Which ending depends on what article precedes it.

## After der/die/das (weak)

| | masc | fem | neut | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nom | -e | -e | -e | -en |
| Akk | **-en** | -e | -e | -en |
| Dat | -en | -en | -en | -en |
| Gen | -en | -en | -en | -en |

Only five slots are `-e`; everything else is `-en`.

## After ein/kein/mein (mixed)

| | masc | fem | neut | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nom | **-er** | -e | **-es** | -en |
| Akk | -en | -e | **-es** | -en |
| Dat | -en | -en | -en | -en |
| Gen | -en | -en | -en | -en |

The difference sits in three cells. `ein` doesn't show gender by itself, so the adjective has to: `ein gut**er** Mann`, `ein gut**es** Kind`.

## With no article (strong)

The adjective takes the ending the definite article would have had:

`gut**er** Wein` (der → -er) · `kalt**es** Wasser` (das → -es) · `mit gut**em** Wein` (dem → -em)

## The shortcut

Ask: **does anything before the adjective already show the case and gender?**

- Yes → the adjective takes `-e` or `-en` (weak).
- No → the adjective must do the job itself, taking the article's ending (strong).
keyRules: Adjective endings depend on the article in front, not just on case.
After a definite article, endings are only -e or -en.
After ein/kein/mein, the masculine nominative is -er and the neuter is -es.
With no article, the adjective takes the ending the definite article would have had.
Predicate adjectives after sein take no ending at all: Das Haus ist groß.

title: Konjunktiv II
summary: Hypotheticals, wishes, and sounding polite instead of blunt.
bodyMd:
Konjunktiv II covers everything unreal: what *would* happen, what you *would like*, what you *could* do.

## The forms you must know cold

| | sein | haben | werden | können | müssen |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | wäre | hätte | würde | könnte | müsste |
| du | wärst | hättest | würdest | könntest | müsstest |
| er/sie/es | wäre | hätte | würde | könnte | müsste |
| wir | wären | hätten | würden | könnten | müssten |

They're built from the Präteritum stem, plus an umlaut, plus `-e` endings.

## Everything else: würde + infinitive

For ordinary verbs, the real Konjunktiv II form sounds archaic (`ich ginge`, `ich käme`). Modern German uses **würde + infinitive** instead:

`Ich **würde** mehr **reisen**, wenn ich Geld hätte.`

But never do this with *sein*, *haben* or the modals — `ich würde haben` is wrong. Use `ich hätte`.

## Unreal conditions

Both halves go into Konjunktiv II:

`**Wenn** ich Zeit **hätte**, **würde** ich mehr lesen.`

## Politeness

This is where you'll use it most in daily life:

`**Könnten** Sie mir helfen?` · `Ich **hätte** gern einen Kaffee.` · `**Wären** Sie so freundlich?`

## Past hypotheticals

Use `hätte` or `wäre` plus the participle:

`Ich **hätte** das nicht **gesagt**.` — *I wouldn't have said that.*
`Wenn ich das **gewusst hätte**, **wäre** ich nicht **gekommen**.`
keyRules: Konjunktiv II expresses hypotheticals, wishes and polite requests.
Use würde + infinitive for most verbs.
Never use würde with sein, haben or the modals — use hätte, wäre, könnte.
Both clauses of an unreal condition go into Konjunktiv II.
Past hypotheticals use hätte/wäre + Partizip II.

examples.de: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich mehr lesen.
examples.en: If I had time, I would read more.

title: The Passive Voice
summary: Shifting the spotlight from the doer to the deed.
bodyMd:
The passive is built with **werden + Partizip II**. It matters in German because formal and technical writing leans on it heavily.

`Das Haus **wird** gebaut.` — *The house is being built.*

## Across the tenses

| Tense | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Präsens | wird + P2 | Das Haus **wird** gebaut. |
| Präteritum | wurde + P2 | Das Haus **wurde** gebaut. |
| Perfekt | ist + P2 + **worden** | Das Haus **ist** gebaut **worden**. |
| with modal | modal + P2 + werden | Das Haus **muss** gebaut **werden**. |

The Perfekt form is the one to watch: the participle of `werden` here is **worden**, not `geworden`. The `ge-` drops.

## Naming the agent

- **von** for a person or active force: `Das Haus wurde **von** einem Architekten geplant.`
- **durch** for a means or cause: `Die Stadt wurde **durch** ein Erdbeben zerstört.`

Most of the time the agent is simply left out — that's the point of the passive.

## Zustandspassiv

`sein + Partizip II` describes a resulting **state**, not an action:

`Die Tür **wird** geöffnet.` — someone is opening it right now.
`Die Tür **ist** geöffnet.` — it stands open.

## Alternatives

German often dodges the passive altogether:

- `**man**` — `**Man** baut hier ein Haus.`
- `sich lassen` — `Das **lässt sich** machen.`
- `sein + zu + infinitive` — `Das **ist zu** machen.`
keyRules: Passive = werden + Partizip II.
In the Perfekt passive, werden's participle is worden, not geworden.
Use von for a personal agent and durch for a means or cause.
sein + Partizip II describes a state; werden + Partizip II describes an action.
man, sich lassen and sein + zu + infinitive are common passive alternatives.

examples.de: Die Arbeit ist schon gemacht worden.
examples.en: The work has already been done.

title: Relative Clauses
summary: Joining sentences with der, die, das — and picking the right case.
bodyMd:
A relative clause adds information about a noun. The relative pronoun takes:

- its **gender and number** from the noun it refers back to,
- its **case** from its job inside the relative clause.

That split is the whole difficulty.

## The pronouns

| | masc | fem | neut | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nom | der | die | das | die |
| Akk | **den** | die | das | die |
| Dat | **dem** | **der** | **dem** | **denen** |
| Gen | **dessen** | **deren** | **dessen** | **deren** |

They match the definite article except in the dative plural (**denen**) and the whole genitive row.

## Working through it

Take *the man whose car is broken*:

1. The noun is `der Mann` → masculine singular.
2. Inside the clause, the man **possesses** the car → genitive.
3. Masculine genitive → **dessen**.

`Der Mann, **dessen** Auto kaputt ist, …`

More examples:

`Der Mann, **der** dort steht, …` — subject → nominative
`Der Mann, **den** ich kenne, …` — object of kennen → accusative
`Der Mann, **dem** ich helfe, …` — helfen takes dative

## With prepositions

The preposition leads, and it decides the case:

`Die Frau, **mit der** ich spreche, …`
`Das Haus, **in dem** ich wohne, …`

## Always

The verb goes to the end, and the clause is always fenced off by commas.
keyRules: Gender and number come from the antecedent; case comes from the relative clause.
Relative pronouns match the definite article except denen (dative plural) and the genitive row.
The verb goes to the end of the relative clause.
A preposition comes before the pronoun and determines its case.
German always separates relative clauses with commas.

examples.de: Das ist der Mann, der mir geholfen hat.
examples.en: That's the man who helped me.

examples.de: Der Film, den wir gesehen haben, war gut.
examples.en: The film we saw was good.

examples.de: Die Frau, mit der ich sprach, ist Ärztin.
examples.en: The woman I spoke with is a doctor.

title: Konjunktiv I & Reported Speech
summary: How German journalism reports what someone said without endorsing it.
bodyMd:
Konjunktiv I signals that you are relaying someone else's claim. It is rare in speech and everywhere in newspapers.

## Formation

Infinitive stem + `-e` endings:

| | sein | haben | gehen | können |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | sei | habe | gehe | könne |
| du | seist | habest | gehest | könnest |
| er/sie/es | **sei** | **habe** | **gehe** | **könne** |
| wir | seien | haben | gehen | können |
| sie/Sie | seien | haben | gehen | können |

`sein` is the irregular one — and the one you'll meet most: `er **sei**`, without the `-e` you'd expect.

## The substitution rule

Look at `wir haben` and `sie haben`: identical to the indicative. A reader couldn't tell it was reported speech.

So when the Konjunktiv I form collides with the indicative, **switch that form to Konjunktiv II**:

`Sie sagen, sie **hätten** keine Zeit.` (not *sie haben*)

That's why real texts mix the two moods — it isn't inconsistency, it's the rule.

## Past reported speech

There is only one past. Use `habe`/`sei` + Partizip II:

`Er sagte, er **sei** früh **gegangen**.`
`Sie erklärte, sie **habe** nichts **gewusst**.`

## In practice

Everyday spoken German just uses `dass` with the indicative:

`Er sagt, **dass** er keine Zeit **hat**.`

Konjunktiv I is a **reading** skill first — recognise it in a newspaper, and you'll know the writer isn't vouching for the claim.
keyRules: Konjunktiv I marks reported speech in formal writing and journalism.
Formed from the infinitive stem + -e endings; sein is irregular (er sei).
When the form matches the indicative, switch to Konjunktiv II instead.
Past reported speech uses habe/sei + Partizip II.
Spoken German prefers dass + indicative.

examples.de: Er sagt, er habe keine Zeit.
examples.en: He says he has no time.

examples.de: Sie behauptet, sie sei krank gewesen.
Die Minister sagten, sie hätten nichts gewusst.
examples.en: The ministers said they knew nothing.

title: Verbs with Fixed Prepositions
summary: Pairings you cannot work out from English — plus the da-/wo- machinery.
bodyMd:
Many German verbs demand a specific preposition and a specific case. The combination is arbitrary and must be learned as a unit: not `warten`, but **warten auf + Akkusativ**.

| Verb | Preposition | Case |
|---|---|---|
| warten | auf | Akk |
| sich freuen | auf (future) / über (now) | Akk |
| sich interessieren | für | Akk |
| denken | an | Akk |
| sich erinnern | an | Akk |
| sich kümmern | um | Akk |
| teilnehmen | an | Dat |
| leiden | unter | Dat |
| gehören | zu | Dat |
| abhängen | von | Dat |
| bestehen | aus (consist of) / auf (insist on) | Dat |

`sich freuen` shows why the preposition matters: `Ich freue mich **auf** das Konzert` (it's still to come) versus `Ich freue mich **über** das Geschenk` (I have it already).

## da- and wo- compounds

Referring back to a **thing**, you cannot say *auf es*. You fuse the preposition with `da-`:

`Ich warte **darauf**.` — *I'm waiting for it.*

Asking about a thing, fuse with `wo-`:

`**Worauf** wartest du?`

Insert an **-r-** when the preposition starts with a vowel: `da**r**auf`, `wo**r**an`, `da**r**über`.

## People are different

For people, keep the preposition and use a normal pronoun:

`**Auf wen** wartest du?` → `Ich warte **auf ihn**.`

## Anticipatory da-

When a `dass`-clause follows, the main clause often needs a `da-` placeholder:

`Ich freue mich **darauf**, **dass** du kommst.`
keyRules: Learn verb + preposition + case as a single unit.
sich freuen auf = look forward to; sich freuen über = be pleased about.
Use da(r)- compounds for things and preposition + pronoun for people.
Insert -r- before a vowel: darauf, woran, darüber.
A following dass-clause often needs an anticipatory da- compound.

examples.de: Ich warte auf den Bus. Ich warte darauf.
examples.en: I'm waiting for the bus. I'm waiting for it.

title: Advanced Connectors
summary: The linking words that make B2 writing read like an adult wrote it.
bodyMd:
At B2 the examiner is looking for connectors beyond `und`, `aber` and `weil`. Three families matter, and each treats word order differently.

## Two-part connectors

| Pair | Meaning |
|---|---|
| entweder … oder | either … or |
| weder … noch | neither … nor |
| sowohl … als auch | both … and |
| nicht nur … sondern auch | not only … but also |
| zwar … aber | admittedly … but |
| je … desto | the … the |

`**Weder** mein Bruder **noch** meine Schwester spricht Deutsch.`

**je … desto** has its own shape: a subordinate clause first (verb last), then `desto` + comparative with the verb second.

`**Je** mehr ich **lerne**, **desto besser verstehe** ich.`

## Adverbial connectors

`trotzdem, deshalb, deswegen, außerdem, allerdings, dennoch, folglich, stattdessen`

These occupy position one, so the verb still comes second and the **subject moves behind it**:

`Es regnete. **Trotzdem gingen wir** spazieren.`

Writing *Trotzdem wir gingen* is the classic mistake.

## Subordinating connectors

`obwohl, während, indem, sodass, falls, sobald, solange, anstatt dass`

Verb to the end, as always:

`**Obwohl** es regnete, **gingen** wir spazieren.`

## Choosing the register

Note how the same idea climbs in formality:

| Spoken | Written | Formal |
|---|---|---|
| weil | da | aufgrund + Gen |
| obwohl | wenngleich | trotz + Gen |
| aber | jedoch | allerdings |
keyRules: Two-part connectors like weder … noch and je … desto must be used complete.
je … desto: subordinate clause with the verb last, then desto + comparative, verb second.
Adverbial connectors (trotzdem, deshalb) keep the verb second, pushing the subject after it.
Subordinating connectors (obwohl, während, sodass) send the verb to the end.
Register climbs from weil to da to aufgrund + genitive.

examples.de: Je mehr ich lerne, desto besser verstehe ich.
examples.en: The more I learn, the better I understand.

examples.de: Es regnete. Trotzdem gingen wir spazieren.
examples.en: It was raining. Nevertheless we went for a walk.

examples.de: Sowohl er als auch sie kommen mit.
examples.en: Both he and she are coming along.
